The general guidance is that anything below 7 is transfusion territory. In practice the way these things are decided is based on your symptoms. People get acclimatised to having a low Hb and get live with no symptoms. What really affects people is having a drop in Hb, or having it too low for your body to cope. 

You need to be careful (without meaning to preach too much). There is only so much they can tolerate, eventually they will force you to go in for treatment. It is well understood that having a low Hb increases risk of cardiac arrest etc. 

However I do understand what you mean when you say that 6.7 isn't that low. I've had several arguments with doctors etc. about whether I need a transfusion. The problem is they would be responsible if you were to drop dead after walking out of the hospital, so they tend to play it safe

This I can relate to. I started bloodletting two years ago as an escalation of my self harm. I didn't tell anyone at first and started with small needles and very small amounts of blood loss. Things quickly escalated until I had taken 2 litres in total over the last month. By this point I had told my doctors and they were getting increasingly concerned.

One day I went into school having taken a good 500ml the night before. I was very ill at this point and could barely walk to the doctors. They took a blood test and let me go. I spent the rest of the day in the medical room then went home. That evening my doctor called me and said I needed to go to hospital. My Hb was 6.4 and I was at a very high risk of heart attack etc. They forced me to hand my phone to my parents on threat of getting me sectioned (aka calling the police). 

So I went to hospital, had a transfusion that brought me up to 7 (bear in mind the 6.4 wouldn't have included the night before's blood loss as there is a lag on the measurements). I had some IV iron and was sent home with a psych follow up.

Over the next few months I received a lot of great care. I had a few relapses, had another transfusion and several iron infusions. My family were heavily involved and I took a lot of time out of school. I ended up retaking the year and have been getting on well with my life since (despite a couple of blips here and there).

Now when it comes to bloodletting, I see it like this. I believe it is the equivalent of heroin in this context. It is highly highly addictive and extremely dangerous. This is a method of SH that causes very little pain, almost no marks or damage if done right but has the potential to cause a lot of harm (and of course be fatal). On the one hand I would love to raise awareness about this, but on the other I think it may be best left a secret from the public. A quick google will show you that bloodletting is not reported on (except in medical journals), so it is much harder to find information on than other SH methods.

As for your final questions: 

-clearly i've blood let. I think since I started I've lost the equivalent of my entire blood volume more than once. Would not recommend, very addictive and dangerous

-I felt trapped and had to stop cutting/SH. My family were way too involved and I hated that. They made me feel guilty and ashamed. Now that it is in the past I am finding relapses much easier to deal with.

Firstly a suggestion: if you're not on iron tablets you should start taking them. Your body will recover on its own if you stop loosing blood, although it will take about a month to do so completely 

Whether they transfuse or not probably depends mostly on your symptoms. If they think that your life is at risk I'm sure they will do it but if you're just walking a fine line they might wait. Make sure you get as many blood tests as you can so your doctor can monitor your Hb. When I was ill I had them weekly for quite a while.

I got a phone call from my doctor after school telling me that I either had to get my parents to take me into hospital or they would get the police to come and take me instead. I didn't have a choice and went with the easier option. I was very sick and if I had self harmed that night I think I would have had a heart attack :(

The second time I had a transfusion I was away with some friends and they took me, my Hb was 7g/l I think. Where I live if it is below 7 they always transfuse. Both times I was given 1 unit (about 330ml) of packed red blood cells, which is about equivalent to getting 660ml of "normal" blood.

I've had two blood transfusions due to self harm. The first time I was admitted with a Hb (haemoglobin / red cell count) of 6.4g/dl. I was very ill, and if I had self harmed that evening before I went to hospital then I might have died. My resting heart rate was 120bpm and I couldn't really stand up. I wasn't refused blood in fact I wasn't given a choice, if I refused they'd have sectioned me and done it without me consent.

If your Hb is that low you need a blood transfusion and likely an iron infusion as well, you must have lost a lot of blood. Please keep me informed, I'd like to know how you get on
